rationale: Bond polarity helps students explain how parts of a macromolecule interact with their surroundings and with other molecules.
Distinguishing forces between molecules from bonds within them helps explain protein folding and interactions in water.
Polarity and charge help explain why different substances cross a lipid membrane by different routes.
Knowing how dissolved particles behave helps interpret solute gradients in an osmosis investigation.
Quantifying the amount of solute per volume helps students compare treatments in an osmosis investigation. Full molarity calculations are optional.
Distinguishing intermolecular attractions from covalent bonds helps explain why DNA strands separate while their backbones remain intact.
Net bond-energy change helps explain how reactions transfer energy and why breaking a bond itself does not release energy.
Conserving each kind of atom while representing a reaction helps students track where matter goes during photosynthesis and respiration.
Atom accounting through photosynthesis and respiration helps distinguish matter cycling from energy flow in an ecosystem model.
Interpreting the pH scale helps students explain what a pH change means in one of the listed environmental-limit examples.
Heating and phase changes can deepen an explanation of freezing as a temperature limit. A survival prediction can use measured tolerance without that mechanism.
Polarity can deepen a comparison that uses lipid envelopes and cell membranes. The standards allow comparisons based on other characteristics.
Enzymes give students a biological catalyst to revisit as an everyday example. The chemistry explanation can use an entirely different catalyst.
Gas exchange in a familiar cellular process can provide a context for revisiting reaction indicators. The chemistry investigation does not depend on that context.
Experience comparing spectral composition helps students interpret line spectra and distinguish emission signatures of elements.
A model of electromagnetic energy transfer adds context to emitted light. The chemistry objective can be explained using energy levels and observed line patterns.
Knowing what fusion changes in a nucleus helps students explain how a new element can form through fusion.
Attraction between opposite charges helps explain ionic bonding and the electrostatic basis of the bonding continuum.
Electric attraction helps students connect observations of bulk properties with interactions at molecular scales.
Electric potential energy can deepen an explanation of energy changes during bond rearrangement. A net bond-energy model can meet the chemistry target.
Distinguishing open and closed systems helps define a calorimetry system and clarify which energy transfers an investigation tracks.
Mechanical energy accounting gives students a conservation example to extend to thermal processes. Heat calculations can be taught without the work-kinetic energy theorem.
A kinetic energy model can deepen discussion of collision energy. Object-scale calculations and mechanical work are beyond the chemistry objective.
A model with mobile electrons helps explain charge transfer by contact and charge redistribution during induction.
Identifying protons and neutrons in the nucleus gives students components to track in models of nuclear change.
Knowing that proton count determines the element helps explain differences in the consequences of alpha, beta, and gamma decay.
Understanding isotopes helps students specify which population is decaying in a half-life model. Average atomic mass calculations are unnecessary.
The fusion portion of the physics comparison revisits a process used in chemistry to explain formation of heavier elements.
Line spectra provide a familiar example of spectral composition. Optics and light investigations need no explanation of atomic transitions.
Modeling light as energy transfer can deepen an explanation of the energy input to photosynthesis. Wave calculations are outside the biology objective.
Spectral composition can enrich a photosynthesis investigation that compares light colors. The biology standard does not require that experimental design.
Distinguishing electromagnetic radiation types can add context for radiation as an environmental source of mutation. The biology standard does not require wave physics.
Knowledge of emissions from radioactive decay can help distinguish radiation sources in an optional context for the variation argument.
Separating inputs and outputs across a system boundary helps students distinguish incoming energy from the matter tracked through an ecosystem.
Energy conservation can clarify why energy transferred out of an ecosystem’s tracked pathways has not disappeared. Mechanical-energy calculations are beyond the standard.
A model of cell membranes and homeostasis helps interpret the effects of transport in an investigation.
Lipid and protein structure helps explain membrane permeability and the role of channels and transporters.
Building blocks and structural properties of nucleic acids and proteins help students explain the steps of gene expression.
Students need a model of meiosis to explain why crossing over or nondisjunction yields new genetic combinations in the specified part of the argument.
Students need to understand what is copied during replication to explain how copying errors produce the listed variants.
Chromosome separation during meiosis supplies the mechanism used to connect Mendel’s laws to variability.
Segregation and independent assortment help justify the assumptions of basic inheritance models.
Models of meiosis and cell division help compare how sexual and asexual reproduction differ in continuity and variation.
Examples of new genetic combinations help students distinguish assortment from other processes contributing to variability.
Recognizing the organization of eukaryotic cells helps students identify the structures that an endosymbiosis argument must explain.
Cell organization and homeostasis provide explicit criteria for comparison with viruses.
Shared characters and recognizable clades give students data and groups to use in a phylogenetic model.
Reading a tree helps connect multiple kinds of evidence with the claim of common ancestry.
Understanding why shared inherited traits support common ancestry helps students select and interpret evidence for phylogenetic trees.
Connecting genes to proteins helps students understand why related species may share protein sequence patterns.
The ecosystem model explicitly includes photosynthesis and respiration, so students need to know their contrasting roles in moving matter and energy.
Evidence about population and biodiversity changes helps students predict responses to disturbance.
A food-web model can help students explain why a disturbance propagates through an ecosystem.
Predicting effects of a disturbance helps identify which consequence an intervention should address.
An organism’s environmental limits help connect an environmental change to potential shifts in species abundance.
Selection and drift require heritable variation for students to model changes in the frequencies of variants.
A population-level model of selection supplies the mechanism for explaining how resistance becomes more common.
Changes in populations provide a mechanism for interpreting patterns of divergence associated with speciation.
Distinguishing the three subatomic particles is necessary to argue which one defines elemental identity.
Students need the connection between proton number and elemental identity to explain how fusion forms another element.
Knowing why atoms can be the same element despite different neutron counts helps explain weighted atomic mass.
Evidence for discrete electron energy states provides context for models of electron configurations.
Electron configuration helps students explain why valence patterns recur down the periodic table.
Electronegativity trends help predict how electrons are shared in a bond.
Electron configurations and ion formation help students reason about sharing or transfer of valence electrons.
Students need bonding and ion-charge models to predict which chemical formulas are consistent with those models.
Recognizing compound formulas supports inference of naming conventions.
Recognizing bond types and polarity helps relate observed properties to competing explanations based on forces.
Students need a link between measurable properties and forces to justify a proposed identification.
A bond model helps connect molecular structure to function in suitable designed materials.
The explanation portion explicitly uses outer electron states, which students need to represent to justify a predicted outcome.
Writing correct formulas helps students distinguish changing an equation’s coefficient from changing a substance.
A balanced equation provides the mole ratios needed to solve reaction stoichiometry problems.
Converting between amount of substance and mass is needed for the specified mass-to-moles and mass-to-mass problems.
Using reaction ratios helps identify which reactant is consumed first. A simple investigation can establish this concept without formal computation.
Observables such as gas evolution give students ways to track changes in reaction progress.
Activation energy helps explain how an alternative pathway changes a reaction rate.
A collision model helps distinguish rate changes from changes in the equilibrium composition.
A pressure-volume-temperature model helps anticipate changes to gas-phase collision conditions in one kind of reaction investigation.
Distinguishing intermolecular attractions from bonds helps explain what the heating-curve plateaus represent alongside the energy input.
Net bond-energy models help interpret the sign of a measured heat transfer for chemical reactions.
Charge and polarity help explain why ions separate or why a molecular solute remains intact as it dissolves.
A model of dissolving helps distinguish dissolving rate from how much solute dissolves at equilibrium.
Mass-to-mole conversion is needed when molarity is obtained from solute mass and solution volume.
Calculating molarity is needed to communicate amounts for preparing a solution at a specified concentration.
Knowing whether solute particles dissociate helps explain differences in their effect on phase transitions.
Reading phase-change behavior for a pure substance provides a baseline for explaining shifts in transition temperatures.
Dissociation gives students a particle-level meaning for percent dissociation and hydronium concentration.
Acid-base models help explain why the observed neutralization occurs.
Reading pH changes helps students interpret the progress of a neutralization investigation.
The one-dimensional objective distinguishes speed from velocity and uses signs to represent direction.
Recognizing position, velocity, and acceleration helps attach physical meaning to features of motion graphs.
Graph interpretation provides another representation for measurements and calculations already made in the motion investigation.
Vector quantities and direction are necessary to resolve and add components of motion.
Independent coordinate motions are analyzed using the one-dimensional relationships.
The direction and relative magnitude of each force matter in a free-body diagram.
Free-body diagrams help distinguish individual forces from the net force used to explain acceleration.
Knowing how net force relates to acceleration helps distinguish equilibrium from nonequilibrium representations.
Estimating forces and resolving components helps calculate acceleration with several forces acting together.
Newton’s laws link the inward force component to the acceleration required for circular motion.
A vector description helps students recognize that velocity can change direction at constant speed.
A gravity model helps students reason about the gravitational contribution in the specified force calculations.
Resolving a force along the displacement helps determine its work.
An energy conservation investigation explicitly uses a closed system, so students must identify its boundary.
Energy accounting gives students a basis for calculating rates of energy transfer.
The momentum objective explicitly connects action-reaction pairs to impulse.
Signed velocities help calculate one-dimensional momentum before and after a collision.
Comparing kinetic energy before and after a collision helps distinguish elastic and inelastic collisions.
A wave model provides wavelength and helps students explain interference and diffraction patterns.
A mechanical wave model helps students explain sound propagation and characterize pitch.
A wave model provides quantities and relationships students can investigate for electromagnetic waves.
Electromagnetic wave properties provide a basis for investigating visible light as part of that spectrum.
Refraction and ray diagrams help interpret observations of light passing through lenses.
Lens investigations revisit the behavior used in the thin-lens calculations and optical diagrams.
A diffraction model helps students predict how pattern geometry changes with wavelength or slit spacing.
The specified comparison needs the gravitational force-distance relationship alongside the electric one.
Attraction and repulsion between charges help explain observed redistribution during induction.
A model of electric forces helps explain how changing separation changes electric potential energy.
Electric potential energy per charge explains the meaning of a voltage difference in a circuit.
Understanding and measuring current helps students relate it to observed changes in magnetic field.
A model of nuclear changes gives students a basis for identifying and comparing types of decay.
Understanding that decay removes nuclei from the parent population clarifies what the half-life model tracks.
